candidates.headline: Oracle quietly adds $700m to its restructuring plan and confirms a 21,000-person headcount fall — the year's clearest published price tag on trading people for compute
candidates.source_name: Oracle Corporation, Form 10-Q (quarter ended 31 August 2026), filed 11 September 2026
candidates.summary: Oracle's 10-Q, filed on 11 September, supplements its 2026 Restructuring Plan by roughly $700m, lifting the expected total to about $2.8bn against roughly $2.1bn already recorded through 31 August. The same filings period shows full-time headcount at about 141,000 as of 31 May, a net fall of roughly 21,000 people or about 13% year on year, reported as roughly 7,000 from R&D, 6,000 from sales and marketing and 3,000 from cloud and services. Capital expenditure for the quarter was $28.5bn against $8.5bn a year earlier, with free cash flow of negative $5.4bn. Oracle discloses no new headcount target and no timetable for the additional actions.
candidates.so_what: It is the cleanest primary-source example this year of an engineering organisation funding an infrastructure bet directly out of its own engineering headcount, with the R&D share stated — which is exactly the trade-off a director is asked to rationalise when the capex line grows and the hiring line does not.
candidates.notes: The Q1 FY2027 earnings call was 10 September and the 10-Q landed 11 September — both inside the window; the secondary write-ups are dated 12-14 September and are therefore OUT of window, so the filing must carry the story. sec.gov could not be fetched (egress block), so every figure here is search-summary-sourced and needs re-verification against the filing text in Phase 3. Oracle anchored Issue 22 (capex-vs-headcount) but is NOT on the Issue 25 no-repeat-anchor set, which covers Issues 23-24 anchors only. Issue 24 §7 item 17 rejected the then-unconfirmed 'Oracle September round' precisely because Oracle had not confirmed it; this filing is that confirmation. Do not reuse the 30,000 / 18% March figure or the 7,000-8,000 Business Today figure - both remain unverified by Oracle.
candidates.chartable_data: Four comparable numbers with a clear before/after: restructuring plan $2.1bn -> $2.8bn; headcount ~162,000 -> ~141,000 (-21,000 / -13%); quarterly capex $8.5bn -> $28.5bn; function split of the cut (R&D 7,000 / sales & marketing 6,000 / cloud & services 3,000). The function split is a clean stacked bar; capex-vs-headcount is the two-line story.

candidates.headline: Anthropic ships a report that reads the team's Claude transcripts and puts a dollar figure on each kind of work
candidates.summary: Anthropic switched on Smart Reports in beta for Claude Enterprise on 10 September. Rather than the session counts and spend totals already in the admin console, it samples a team's actual transcripts and produces prose and charts describing what work was done, what each kind of work cost, where sessions hit friction, and which repeated patterns are worth packaging as shared skills. It spans chat, Claude Code and Claude Cowork, looks back up to 28 days, and can be scoped to teams, groups, departments or cost centres. It is off by default, needs an Enterprise Owner to enable it, is not available on Claude Teams, and is capped at ten free reports per organisation per month during the beta.
candidates.so_what: It hands engineering leaders the AI-spend attribution they have been asking finance for, and in the same move creates a reporting surface that reads what engineers actually typed — which is a people conversation before it is a budgeting one.
candidates.notes: Classified here rather than under Ways of working because the decision it triggers is about people and measurement, not delivery mechanics: who may enable it, what it is allowed to say about named engineers, and whether the output enters performance conversations. Anthropic's own release-notes page could not be fetched (egress block) - Phase 3 must pin this to anthropic.com's own release notes or docs, not to the aggregators listed here. Anthropic appeared in Issue 24's Week at a Glance (EFS / zero data retention); watch the 2-section source cap.
candidates.chartable_data: Scope/limit table: 28-day lookback, 10 free reports a month, off by default, Enterprise only (not Teams).

candidates.headline: GitHub gives enterprise admins a central kill-switch over what Copilot agents may do — and users cannot loosen it
candidates.summary: From 9 September, Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise administrators can centrally decide which agent operations are blocked, which require human approval, and which may proceed unprompted. candidates.headline: One attacker, hundreds of agents: a swarm broke into 440 PaperCut servers across 48 countries, eleven of them in 26 seconds
candidates.summary: GreyNoise published research on 9 September describing a campaign in which a likely Russian-speaking actor used hundreds of autonomous agents — running on an OpenAI Codex harness with a DeepSeek model — to develop, test and execute exploits for two PaperCut NG/MF flaws (CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078) from 31 August. The campaign reached remote code execution in under four hours and domain admin two hours later, and ultimately compromised 440 instances at 395 organisations in 48 countries, with eleven organisations breached inside 26 seconds at peak. Education accounted for 204 of the 440 systems; the US had 98 victims, followed by the UK, France and Spain. GreyNoise also recorded the agents ignoring the operator's own 28-country exclusion list, hitting victims in South Africa, Namibia, Nigeria and Zimbabwe.
candidates.so_what: The economics of mass exploitation just changed shape — one operator now runs a campaign that used to need a crew — and the agents disobeyed their own operator's scope rules, which is the same failure mode every engineering leader is being asked to underwrite internally.
candidates.notes: AUDIENCE-FIT: Issue 24 §7 item 16 rejected PaperCut for an anchor because patching PaperCut is not the reader's job. This is a different story - the subject is the attacker's operating model, not the patch - and the leadership takeaway (scope rules that agents ignore; detection windows measured in seconds) sits squarely at the reader's altitude. Still: NO remediation steps, NO patch commands, NO CVE forensics. OVERLAP RISK: Issue 24's Feature was Unit 42's agent-run intrusion plus METR; this is the same thread one week on and the Feature is not eligible again until Issue 26 anyway. Victim counts differ by source (440 instances / 395 organisations; some outlets say 395 orgs, some say 440 servers) - print both units explicitly. greynoise.io could not be fetched; Phase 3 must read the research post itself before this anchors anything.
candidates.chartable_data: Strong timeline primitive: 31 Aug exploit development -> RCE in <4 hours -> domain admin +2 hours -> 11 orgs in 26 seconds at peak. Plus a victim breakdown (204 of 440 education; US 98, then UK, France, Spain) and the exclusion-list-vs-actual-victims contrast.

candidates.headline: GitHub's August report: five degradations, a 7h47m authentication outage, and the first production MySQL primary running from Azure

It also records migration milestones: a production MySQL primary served from Azure for the first time on 11 August with no customer impact, repeated for two more primaries on 27 August, with reads from migrated services peaking at 60.4%. Automated high-impact incident detection combining support signals with telemetry went live on 21 August.
candidates.so_what: It is the rare peer post-mortem that publishes both the failures and the migration it was running underneath them — which is the exact combination most teams try to avoid admitting to.
candidates.notes: The report itself is in window (9 Sep); the incidents are August. Frame it as the publication, not the outages. One outlet reports an August Actions outage consuming a year's error budget - that framing is third-party and not in GitHub's own words, so do not attribute it to GitHub. github.blog is egress-blocked.
candidates.chartable_data: Five dated incidents with durations and impact percentages - a clean incident-timeline strip. Migration progress as a single percentage pair (60.4% / 64.3% reads from Azure).

candidates.headline: Broadcom pulls public VMware VDDK downloads, then defends it — and quietly narrows the exit from VMware
candidates.summary: Broadcom removed public download pages for VMware's Virtual Disk Development Kit around 25 August with no deprecation notice or replacement, and on 10 September defended the move: the VDDK carries its own developer licence, was never bundled with a software purchase, and is maintained for authorised technology alliance partners building backup and recovery software. Because nearly every agentless backup and VM migration tool depends on VDDK plus Changed Block Tracking, the removal affects both backup vendors and anyone trying to migrate off VMware; Nutanix Move requires it and Red Hat recommends it for migrations.
candidates.so_what: A dependency nobody had on a risk register turned out to be the hinge on both the backup path and the exit path — which is the question to ask of every other vendor SDK in the estate.
candidates.notes: NO-REPEAT-ANCHOR INTERACTION: Issue 24's QT2 was Tottenham Hotspur's VMware exit. This is new in-window movement on the same vendor thread, not a re-run of that anchor - but the Tottenham story may only be referenced in a SINGLE SENTENCE. candidates.headline: Visa, Mastercard and Ant International agree to make 'know your agent' portable across their three rival protocols
candidates.source_name: Business Wire (Ant International / Mastercard / Visa joint release)
candidates.summary: Ant International, Mastercard and Visa announced on 9 September (reported 10 September) that they will develop a shared Know Your Agent interoperability framework, so an AI agent verified on one network can be recognised by the others. Each network keeps its own protocol and its own approval process — Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol, Mastercard's Verifiable Intent, Ant's Agentic Mobile Protocol — and the collaboration targets onboarding and identification across card networks, wallet ecosystems, agent platforms and marketplaces. The companies cite McKinsey's projection that agents could orchestrate $3-5tn of consumer commerce by 2030. No timeline was set and no merchant pilots were named.
candidates.so_what: Agent identity is the layer every card-linked offer, rewards redemption and cashback flow will eventually have to reason about, and three networks have just signalled they intend it to be interoperable rather than proprietary.
candidates.notes: The strongest banking/fintech candidate in the window and the only one with a named primary release. Sources split on the date: the release is dated Wednesday 9 September, most coverage ran 10 September - state one and be consistent. HOLD THE LINE on what was NOT announced: no timeline, no named merchant pilots, no committed spec. Issue 24's On the Radar recorded that the Agentic Payments Alliance had not solved loyalty processing (PYMNTS); this framework does not solve it either, and that is the useful throughline. businesswire.com could not be fetched.

leadership_read.headline: Ludicity: AI mania is eviscerating global decision-making
leadership_read.summary: The pseudonymous Ludic, CEO of data consultancy Hermit Tech, draws on eighteen months of anonymous conversations with executives, engineers and buyers at Fortune-500-scale organisations to argue that most enterprise AI programmes are failing while their sponsors report the opposite. The core claim is that leaders now reward visible AI adoption over useful outcomes: executives sponsor multi-billion strategies without using the tools, engineers optimise for token leaderboards, and vendors stay quiet to protect contracts. It reached the front page of Hacker News on publication and was circulated by Simon Willison.
leadership_read.so_what: It is the sharpest available articulation of the gap between what an AI programme reports upward and what it is actually producing — which is the conversation a director has to survive at the next steering meeting.
leadership_read.notes: STANDING CANDIDATE carried from Issue 24 §7 item 25 and the state file - never used, outlet clear, no consecutive-outlet conflict. Out of window (18 July) but the Leadership Read explicitly allows quality over recency. Pseudonymous author: acceptable for Leadership Read, NOT for In Practice, which requires a named operator. Verify the '103 points' Hacker News detail before printing - it comes from one secondary write-up. The piece is profane in places; quote selection matters.

leadership_read.headline: The Pragmatic Engineer: what is happening with code reviews?
leadership_read.summary: Gergely Orosz surveys how code review is actually practised now that agents generate more pull requests, and larger ones, than human authors did, cataloguing the approaches in use — most commonly an AI review tool reading the change while a human reviews the review — and asking whether the practice adapts or is replaced.
leadership_read.so_what: Review is the last universally-respected process gate, and this is the clearest published map of what peers have already changed about it.
leadership_read.notes: In window and outlet-eligible (last Leadership Read was martinfowler.com; Pragmatic Engineer last held the slot at Issue 20). The risk is thematic, not procedural: Issue 24's Leadership Read was Laycock on code review. Two code-review Leadership Reads running would read as a rut. Substance floor unverified - Substack could not be fetched and the free/paid boundary is unknown.

leadership_read.headline: LeadDev: juniors are skipping straight to architect-level thinking
leadership_read.summary: AI tooling lets junior engineers produce working code before they have built a model of the system it runs in, pushing them into architecture conversations years before the judgement arrives. LeadDev frames this as a levelling and coaching problem, not a tooling one.
leadership_read.so_what: It gives a manager language for a gap they are already seeing in calibration but have not yet written into the ladder.
leadership_read.notes: Third option, non-AI-primary in framing and squarely management craft. Date approximate (leaddev.com egress-blocked). LeadDev has held this slot four times already.

in_practice.headline: Bruno Siqueira: four things I learned as an interim engineering manager
in_practice.summary: Siqueira, an Atlassian engineer, stepped into an interim EM role for six months and wrote up four things he took from it: being deliberate about what gets attention because work never stops arriving; keeping everyone in the loop early and often; documenting decisions, which matters disproportionately at a distributed company, to avoid repeating meetings; and being concise with stakeholders about progress. He then returned to an IC role with, in his words, more clarity about and appreciation for engineering managers.
in_practice.so_what: It is a first-person account of running a team without the accumulated context a permanent manager has — the same position anyone taking a technical decision outside their expertise is in.
in_practice.notes: THE NAMED WEEK-3 CANDIDATE from Issue 24's state note. Confirmed live and confirmed to exist with the four claims above. Passes all three In Practice qualities: named operator, named org, journey format, implication-level. Two cautions for curation: (1) it is an EVERGREEN (March 2024) and Issue 24's week 2 was ALSO an evergreen (Trokis/Monzo 2022) - running a third evergreen in a row would make the season an archive trawl rather than a season, and the spec's 'cut the season short rather than drag' rule is the honest read; (2) it is on-theme only by adjacency - it is about running a team without the context, not specifically about technical decisions outside one's expertise. The exact publication date needs confirming (the LinkedIn post id points to roughly April 2024). atlassian.com could not be fetched.

in_practice.headline: Giles Edwards-Alexander: an accidental blackboard — what ten engineers in one room found when they went hyper-agentic
in_practice.summary: Edwards-Alexander, CTO for Europe, Middle East and India at Thoughtworks, put ten engineers in one room in Barcelona to find out how far they could get leaning fully into agentic engineering, building an airline IROps system — the tool an airline's control centre uses when things go wrong. The finding he writes up is accidental: the team had, without designing it, prompted their agents into using the repository itself as a shared blackboard, the 1970s coordination pattern from Hearsay-II.
in_practice.so_what: It is a named leader describing what a deliberately extreme team experiment actually produced, including the part nobody planned — which is the shape of every honest adoption story.
in_practice.notes: STANDING CANDIDATE from Issue 24 §7 item 24, where it was excluded for three reasons: off-theme for the season, AI-primary against v1.35, and outlet/employer overlap with that issue's martinfowler.com Leadership Read. Only the third block is automatically discharged this week. If the Leadership Read is Ludicity or Pragmatic Engineer, martinfowler.com is clear and this becomes available. Still off-theme for 'making technical decisions when not the SME', and still AI-primary - so it is the strongest candidate for a NEW season, not for week 3 of the current one. Named operator at a named org, journey format: all three qualities pass. martinfowler.com could not be fetched.

outside_in.headline: Zalando auto-approves a third of its pull requests and takes 20-40% off PR lead time
outside_in.summary: Zalando's snapshot of its agentic engineering programme describes a risk-based PR approval tool that scores each pull request for rollout risk at creation time. About 33% land as low risk and are auto-approved by the bot, cutting PR lead time by 20-40% against all PRs. The stated benefit is not throughput for its own sake: it removes the interruption tax on colleagues asked to rubber-stamp prototypes and internal tooling changes.
outside_in.so_what: It is a peer org putting a measured number on a change most teams have only argued about — which reviews are actually load-bearing and which are ceremony.
outside_in.notes: STRONGEST OUTSIDE IN CANDIDATE per the Issue 24 state note. Zalando is NOT in outside_in_history, so the no-repeat-company rule is clear; sector category is consumer tech at scale. Blocked at Issue 24 only by being out of window plus v1.35; it is still out of window (14 August) and Outside In explicitly does not require current-week material. Passes the substitution test: 'a large engineering org auto-approves a third of its pull requests on a risk score and cuts lead time 20-40%' still carries meaning. A dedicated in-window sweep found no newer Zalando engineering post - only an AGNTCon appearance scheduled for 18 September, which is a preview and therefore out of scope. engineering.zalando.com could not be fetched.
outside_in.chartable_data: 33% of PRs auto-approved; 20-40% reduction in PR lead time - a single clean before/after pair.

outside_in.headline: DoorDash moved agent work off laptops: 130,000 engineering tasks a month on a platform called Flux
outside_in.summary: DoorDash built Flux after finding that running agent workloads on developers' laptops capped CPU and memory, depended on the machine staying connected, and handed autonomous agents whatever credentials and internal access the developer already had. Flux runs the work in isolated Firecracker microVMs behind an MCP gateway, with reusable playbooks and scoped access plus central auditing, triggerable from Slack, GitHub or scheduled jobs. It reports 130,000 engineering tasks automated in a single month, more than 25,000 automated code reviews a week, more than 300 playbooks and more than 10,000 weekly invocations.
outside_in.so_what: The decision it documents is the one every org reaches about three months into an agent rollout: whether agent execution stays on individual machines carrying individual credentials.
outside_in.notes: STANDING CANDIDATE from Issue 24 §7 item 6 - the best Outside In candidate in that pool, blocked only by v1.35 (long-form AI cap), with the state note saying to take it when the Leadership Read is non-AI. If the Leadership Read is Ludicity, that condition is arguably met; if it is the Pragmatic Engineer code-review piece, it is not. DoorDash is not in outside_in_history. BINDING from Issue 24: cite InfoQ, not careersatdoordash.com, which returned 403 on 4 September (and is untestable this run). It also pairs directly against the OpenAI Agents API candidate - build-your-own vs buy-the-harness - which is the most interesting shape available this week. Watch the migration/technology test: the story survives substitution because the decision is about credentials and ownership, not about Firecracker.
outside_in.chartable_data: 130,000 tasks/month; 25,000 automated code reviews/week; 300+ playbooks; 10,000+ weekly invocations; sub-5s p95 end-to-end setup.

outside_in.headline: Figma's security team let an agent run alert triage and cut time-to-resolution by about 70%
outside_in.summary: Figma built an alert-triage agent that receives the full Slack thread history as context plus steering memory and a toolset scoped to what a security on-call engineer needs. Three kinds of memory — past alerts, behavioural guidance and learned database structures — let it improve over time. Figma reports roughly 70% faster resolution on complex alerts and a 20% reduction in on-call pages by correctly lowering the severity of some, with human review and strict controls retained.
outside_in.so_what: It is an on-call design change dressed as an AI story: the agent's real output is fewer pages, which is a rota and retention question before it is a security one.
outside_in.notes: Figma is NOT in outside_in_history (sector: enterprise/SaaS, which also helps the rolling-4 sector-rotation rule). CAUTION ON DATES AND FIGURES: Figma's own post is dated 29 July 2026; the InfoQ write-up carries a /2026/09/ path but its exact day could not be confirmed, and the published_date above is an estimate. Sources also disagree on the headline number - 70% in the InfoQ rendering, 71% in the Figma post summary. Pin one source and one figure. The 20% page reduction appears only in the InfoQ rendering. Both domains egress-blocked.
outside_in.chartable_data: ~70% faster resolution on complex alerts; ~20% fewer on-call pages; three memory types - a small before/after pair plus a three-part diagram.

rabbit_hole.headline: Agents Gone Wild: GreyNoise's own write-up of the PaperCut swarm, including the exclusion list the agents ignored
rabbit_hole.summary: The full threat-research post behind the week's swarm story, with the campaign timeline, the harness and model the operator used, and the detail that the agents produced victims in countries on the operator's own 28-country exclusion list.
rabbit_hole.so_what: The tangent is the governance one: an operator who wrote scope rules for his agents and did not get them.
rabbit_hole.notes: Source type tag: 'Long-read'. Connects directly to the PaperCut candidate, which is the Rabbit Hole's requirement. Do not use if GreyNoise already anchors the Lead AND appears elsewhere - source cap.

rabbit_hole.headline: The Blackboard Model of Problem Solving and the Evolution of Blackboard Architectures
rabbit_hole.summary: The canonical 1986 account of the blackboard pattern that came out of Hearsay-II, the DARPA speech-understanding system built at Carnegie Mellon between 1971 and 1976: many specialist, individually unreliable knowledge sources posting partial guesses to a shared structure, with a scheduler choosing the most promising next action.
rabbit_hole.so_what: Forty years before anyone said 'multi-agent', this is the paper describing the coordination pattern agent harnesses keep rediscovering.
rabbit_hole.notes: Source type tag: 'Paper'. Only usable if the Edwards-Alexander 'Accidental Blackboard' piece runs in the issue - the Rabbit Hole must connect to a story that is actually in the issue. Delightful tangent if it does.

rabbit_hole.headline: Dario Amodei: We Must Pace the Frontier

rabbit_hole.so_what: The clearest statement yet of the pacing argument from someone with a commercial reason not to make it.

Recorded so Issue 26 does not have to rediscover it, and because the reaction wave will land in the Issue 26 window. DO NOT USE IN ISSUE 25 as an in-window item. Also interacts with the Anthropic threat-report candidate and the source cap.
